photo_seen.author: Pixelkaktus

leads.verify_notes: Register only (city Naturdenkmal ND 18, Beschluss 601/96); Wikidata item has two Commons photos and a Commons category. Register height 15 m; no girth or age. Life: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist observation 2026-08-30 at the spot. Manor history (de.wikipedia): first mentioned 1350; Bach's Bauernkantate premiered here 30 Aug 1742; publisher Christian Bernhard Tauchnitz bought the estate in 1848. The page does NOT say the ginkgo dates from any of these owners (bridge-claim trap, no age basis). A Flatterulme (ND 17, 12 m) stands about 45 m away in the same estate at 51.31471,12.32996, not delivered separately. Access is the open question; potential hard-rule-10 issue.
leads.story:
Bach's Peasant Cantata had its first performance at this manor on 30 August 1742, and a ginkgo now stands on its grounds as one of Leipzig's protected natural monuments. The Rittergut Kleinzschocher is first mentioned in 1350, and the publisher Christian Bernhard Tauchnitz bought the estate in 1848. None of those dates belongs to the tree. No source we have found says when the ginkgo was planted, or by which owner, and we are not going to guess.

What the city's register does say is short. It lists the tree as natural monument 18, protected under council resolution 601/96, and gives its height as 15 metres. No girth, no age. A photograph from 2019 and a naturalist's observation in August 2026 show that it is still standing.

Ginkgo is the oldest tree lineage on earth still growing, a species that was already old when the dinosaurs were young, and it ended up in European parks and manor gardens as a curiosity from East Asia. Here it shares the old estate with a second protected tree, a European white elm about 45 metres away, natural monument 17.

In November the leaves turn a clean butter yellow and tend to drop within days of each other. If you know when this one was planted, or how big it is round the trunk, tell us.
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its fan-shaped leaves, a ginkgo about 15 metres tall on the Rittergut Kleinzschocher grounds at Kantatenweg 31. The protected white elm stands about 45 metres away.

best_time.label: November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn yellow and drop almost together
